glosses: Rendre une plante naine.

examples.text: Un arrivage de plantes du Japon, la plupart remarquables par leur forme naine et tourmentée, qui donne une idée de l’art avec lequel les horticulteurs japonais savent naniser les plantes.

glosses: Any member of a race of beings from (especially Scandinavian and other Germanic) folklore, usually depicted as having some sort of supernatural powers and being skilled in crafting and metalworking, often as short with long beards, and sometimes as clashing with elves.

examples.text: Nidavellir, which is sometimes called Svartalfheim, where the dwarfs (who are also known as dark elves) live beneath the mountains and build their remarkable creations.

glosses: A person of short stature, often one whose limbs are disproportionately small in relation to the body as compared with typical adults, usually as the result of a genetic condition.
An animal, plant or other thing much smaller than the usual of its sort.

examples.text: dwarf tree
dwarf honeysuckle

glosses: A dwarf star.

examples.text: But none of those brown dwarfs were speeding along on a trajectory that would carry them out of the galaxy like “runaway” hypervelocity stars observed by astronomers in the last two decades.

glosses: Miniature.

examples.text: The specimen is a very dwarf form of the plant.
It is possible to grow the plants as dwarf as one desires.

glosses: To render (much) smaller, turn into a dwarf (version).
To make appear (much) smaller, puny, tiny; to be much larger than.

examples.text: The newly-built skyscraper dwarfs all older buildings in the downtown skyline.
The train bursts from Rusher Cutting Tunnel with explosive violence, the engine's exhaust soaring high into the air, but dwarfed by the mighty limestone cliffs on either side.
In the past two years, NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope has located nearly 3,000 exoplanet candidates ranging from sub-Earth-sized minions to gas giants that dwarf our own Jupiter.

glosses: To make appear insignificant.

examples.text: Bach dwarfs all other composers.

glosses: To become (much) smaller.
To hinder from growing to the natural size; to make or keep small; to stunt.

examples.text: At present the whole sex is in a manner dwarfed and shrunk - into a race of beauties that seems almost another species
Even the most common moral ideas and affections […] would be stunted and dwarfed, if cut off from a spiritual background.

glosses: To cause to become smaller.

examples.text: The dryer shrank my sweater.
The bottom line is this: To shrink your gut, you need to start listening to it.

glosses: To become smaller; to contract.

examples.text: This garment will shrink when wet.
I have not found that water, by mixture of ashes, will shrink or draw into less room.
And shrink like parchment in consuming fire.
Since 1982, it has shrunk by 250 meters.
When they took over the 1000 'Flying Scotsman' from May 1979, the journey from London to Edinburgh shrank to just 4hrs 37mins - including a stop at Newcastle.

glosses: To cower or flinch.

examples.text: Molly shrank away from the blows of the whip.

glosses: To draw back; to withdraw.

examples.text: The Libyc Hammon ſhrinks his horn,

glosses: To withdraw or retire, as from danger.

examples.text: What happier natures shrink at with affright, / The hard inhabitant contends is right.
They assisted us against the Thebans when you shrank from the task.
The other patients in the ward, all but the Texan, shrank from him with a tenderhearted aversion from the moment they set eyes on him the morning after the night he had been sneaked in.

glosses: To move back or away, especially because of fear or disgust.
Shrinkage; contraction; recoil.

examples.text: Yet almost with, with sudden shrink, That I had less to praise.

glosses: A psychiatrist or psychotherapist.

examples.text: You need to see a shrink, you crazy fool.
My shrink said that he was an enabler, bad for me.
I went to a shrink to analyze my dreams / She says it's lack of sex that's bringing me down
